speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: When the Cess Act was first enacted, cess was a broad-based tax imposed on sales made and charges levied or collected by tourist hotels, food establishments and public houses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: These refer to strategic events that entail higher staging costs using public funding and would enhance Singapore’s global branding, while bringing economic benefits to the country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In this Bill, we propose three categories of amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The first is to clarify the scope of cess, and the second is to update the scope of the Cess Act to keep pace with business developments and industry trends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The third is to enhance existing administrative requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Our aim is to provide clarity and ensure a consistent basis of taxation for all parties that are liable to pay cess.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: There is no change to the underlying principle of our cess policy, which is to ensure that business groups likely to benefit commercially from a strategic tourism event play their part in defraying the costs of organising the event.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The new definition of “transaction” under clause 2, as read with clause 4, seeks to clarify what is subject to cess.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For example, in the context of cess for tourist hotels during the Singapore Grand Prix, the value of the hotel room will be used to calculate cess, regardless of the mode of payment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Whether the customer pays using credit card, cash or vouchers, the hotel needs to pay cess based on the value of the hotel room.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The same rationale applies to rooms which are redeemed using loyalty points under the hotel’s membership programme, or those offered by the hotel as part of wedding or corporate packages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The hotel will need to pay cess based on the value of the hotel room.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Given the evolving business practices and variety of room packages that are offered by different hotels, this approach will ensure a consistent basis of taxation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: There can be other commercial entities which benefit from a strategic tourism event, but are not tourist hotels, tourist food establishments and tourist public houses which are the taxable persons in the current Cess Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Hence, we want to update the Act so that our laws can be applied fairly as business models continue to evolve, and we see the emergence of a greater variety of products and services that serve similar needs in the tourism landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The changes are proposed under clauses 2 and 4 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The imposition of cess will continue to be targeted and calibrated, based on the current set of policy considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will consult the industry and stakeholder groups if there are plans in the future to gazette new tourism events or to impose cess on new categories of tourism event establishments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We are also proposing a few amendments to enhance existing administrative requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clauses 5 and 7 will enable the Chief Executive of the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) and other authorised persons to obtain information from any persons for the purpose of providing views to the Minister on the cess policy, and to administer or enforce the Cess Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In the process of amending the Cess Act, MTI and STB launched a public consultation exercise in March 2018 and conducted an engagement session with hoteliers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Their feedback and comments were considered and addressed during the consultation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tourism is a major industry that not only has knock-off effects for local businesses, but also for our city branding and international reputation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have done well in many aspects, especially in urban and heritage conservation, to make Singapore a unique destination with an old-world colonial port city charm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Balancing this, we have also become a global city of choice for meetings, conventions and events with iconic developments, such as Marina Bay, and signature events, such as the Formula One night race.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Cess Act has been closely tied with Formula One.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cess collection has been limited to hotels benefiting from the F1 race.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this amendment Bill, it looks like the last 10 years of taxing hotels to fund the F1 race was a successful experiment to see whether such a tax was viable to fund a tourist event and would not hamper the growth of tourism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could the Government give greater details of the results of the experiment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What has been the principle involved in identifying which hotels pay cess for F1?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why has cess collection not been extended to tourist food establishments and public houses?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, I would like to sound a caution on over-expansion of cess collection, though the Government has allayed fears by saying that there are no immediate plans to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even with F1, expanding cess collection beyond hotels will have to be done in a judicious manner so as not to inadvertently hurt local businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may be trickier, for example, to identify using geographical markers tourist food establishments that are benefiting specially from F1, especially when many establishments actually make losses during the event due to road closures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other question I have for this amendment Bill is, where does the collected cess go?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the cess collection is very targeted and the specified aim for cess collection is to fund strategic tourist events, there is a case for ringfencing the collected cess to further the national interest of tourist development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some quarters among the public have been critical of F1 as an exclusive event enjoyed by the global and local elites.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order to allay this perception, we need to show more tangible benefits arising from the event, spread the proceeds from the event to the sector as a whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than it being symbolic, we could also do something for retail businesses affected by the road closures and traffic redirection linked to F1 and, in the future, other tourist mega-events.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could have a special innovation and marketing scheme under the Tourism Development Fund that targets affected retail businesses to see how they can reinvent themselves for the tourist visitors and market themselves during this special event.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The role of the Government would be to make sure the winnings are more equitably distributed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And tourism cess collection is a good instrument in this respect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we need to address perceptions and mitigate the inadvertent losses suffered by the losers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To this end, tying the cess collection more directly to the Tourism Development Fund could kill many birds with one stone.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The decision was made after careful consideration of the projected costs and benefits from a national perspective.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We assessed the overall benefits to outweigh the costs, including indirect costs, such as inconveniences due to road closures during the race period.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Assoc Prof Daniel Goh pointed out, there are also indirect benefits through the international media coverage and high global viewership, which boost Singapore’s image as a vibrant and dynamic city.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: After MTI amended the Act in 2008, only gazetted tourist hotels needed to pay cess during the period of the Singapore F1 race.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are hotels which cater mainly to tourists.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have not extended cess collection to food establishments and public houses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In making the assessment, we are guided by the principle of our cess policy, which is to ensure that business groups which are likely to benefit commercially from a strategic tourism event would play their part in defraying the costs of organising these events.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Daniel Goh that any expansion in cess collection has to be done in a judicious manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The amount of cess collected from gazetted tourist hotels varies each year, depending on the industry’s performance that year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Historically, the F1 hotel cess collected has averaged about $13 million each year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The cess collected goes to STB and supplements the Tourism Development Fund to support the costs of the F1 project.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the years, Government agencies have worked closely with the race promoter and affected stakeholders to improve the race execution.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For instance, we have halved the number of days for road closures from 12 days when we first started in 2008 to six days in 2017.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The opening of the Circle Line and Downtown Line stations also increased accessibility to the race vicinity during the F1 period.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To help tourism stakeholders, including retailers and food and beverage (F&B) outlets, capitalise on the buzz created by the F1 race each year, STB works closely with them to launch the Grand Prix Season Singapore (GPSS).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is a season of lifestyle events complementing the race experience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Businesses have also used GPSS as an opportunity to innovate and testbed new commercial concepts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond F1, we started the Kickstart Fund, with a budget of $10 million, to encourage more ground-up initiatives from the industry to try out innovative event concepts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For instance, the Fund has helped to launch new events, such as the Spartan Race and Singapore Cocktail Festival.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We hope to collaborate with the industry to support more events in the coming years.
